Datalab 
 
 State of the Art models for Document Intelligence 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 Surya

Surya is a 689M param document OCR and layout VLM with these features:

- Accuracy - scores 85.9 on OmniParseBench, the highest of the open models under 1B parameters we have scored, and 83.7% on olmOCR-bench
- Speed - throughput of 4.5 pages/s on one H100 at 192 DPI, 1.7x Surya 2 with MTP (see Throughput)
- Multilingual - scores 74.9% on an internal benchmark set of 91 languages (more here)
- Layout analysis ( Table , Picture , SectionHeader , Equation , Form , etc.) with reading order and token-count estimates
- Tables as HTML ( , , , ) with merged cells as colspan / rowspan 
- Zero heavy local ML dependencies - surya-ocr is a lightweight client/orchestrator that talks to vllm (Docker / Podman), llama-server (llama.cpp), or mlx vlm.server (Apple Silicon)

 Try Datalab's Managed Platform

Our managed platform uses Surya, our highest accuracy model Chandra, and other models.

The Datalab API turns documents into verifiable knowledge your agents act on. Every result traces back to its page and position, and one API can parse, extract, fill and edit documents.

Get started with about 5,000 free convert pages every month (work email) — sign up (takes under 30 seconds) or try our free public playground.

 Commercial usage

The Surya code is licensed under Apache 2.0. The model weights use a modified AI Pubs Open Rail-M license (free for research, personal use, and startups under $5M funding/revenue). For broader commercial licensing of the model weights, visit our pricing page here.

 Inference backend prerequisites

Surya auto-spawns the inference server on first use, using vllm (NVIDIA GPU) or llama.cpp (CPU / Apple Silicon):

- NVIDIA GPU: Docker or Podman plus the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.
- CPU / Apple Silicon: the llama-server binary from llama.cpp:
 

 Upgrading from Surya v1

If you have v1 code, migrate to SuryaInferenceManager :

 

What's different:
- SuryaInferenceManager replaces FoundationPredictor . The same manager instance is shared across LayoutPredictor , RecognitionPredictor , and TableRecPredictor .
- Output schemas return structured blocks (with html , label , polygon , bbox , reading order , confidence ); layout boxes include count (token budget estimate); table recognition returns full HTML tables ( ... with colspan / rowspan ).

 Usage

Surya 2.5 runs layout, OCR, and table recognition through a single VLM. The inference manager spawns a server for you on first use; you can also point it at an existing OpenAI-compatible server via SURYA INFERENCE URL= 

- Inspect the settings in surya/settings.py . You can override any setting via environment variables (e.g. SURYA INFERENCE BACKEND=vllm ).

 Server lifecycle ( --keep server )

By default each CLI command spawns the VLM server on startup and shuts it down on
exit — so running several commands in a row pays the startup (and, on GPU, the
model-load) cost every time. Pass --keep server to leave the server running
so later commands attach to it instead of re-spawning:

 

 --keep server works on every command. Stop the server when you're done
( docker stop / podman stop the surya-vllm- container, or kill the llama-server 
process), or set SURYA INFERENCE KEEP ALIVE=1 to make keep-alive the default.

 Interactive App

 surya gui launches a self-contained interactive web viewer in your browser (with zero extra dependencies) where you can drop PDFs or images and inspect layout boxes, reading order, KaTeX-rendered math, HTML tables, and JSON page by page across all Surya modes ( Full-Page OCR , Block OCR , Layout , and Table Rec ):

 

 OCR (text recognition)

This command writes out a results.json file with the detected blocks, labels, bboxes, and HTML content:

 

- DATA PATH can be an image, pdf, or folder of images/pdfs
- --stdout writes the JSON result directly to stdout instead of saving to a directory (ideal for AI agents and shell pipelines)
- --block mode runs layout detection first and then OCRs each detected block crop individually (default is single-call full-page OCR)
- --recursive / -r recursively searches subdirectories when DATA PATH is a folder
- --images will save images of the pages and detected blocks (optional)
- --output dir specifies the directory to save results to instead of the default
- --page range specifies the page range to process in the PDF, specified as a single number, a comma separated list, a range, or comma separated ranges - example: 0,5-10,20 .

install.title: Installation
install.html:
Install with:

pip install surya-ocr

Inference backend prerequisites

Surya auto-spawns the inference server on first use, using vllm (NVIDIA GPU) or llama.cpp (CPU / Apple Silicon):

  • NVIDIA GPU: Docker or Podman plus the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.
  • CPU / Apple Silicon: the llama-server binary from llama.cpp:
    brew install llama.cpp     # macOS
# or grab a release from https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases

Upgrading from Surya v1

If you have v1 code, migrate to SuryaInferenceManager:

from PIL import Image
from surya import SuryaInferenceManager, RecognitionPredictor

manager = SuryaInferenceManager()              # auto-spawns vllm or llama-server
rec = RecognitionPredictor(manager)
predictions = rec([Image.open("page.png")])

What's different:

  • SuryaInferenceManager replaces FoundationPredictor. The same manager instance is shared across LayoutPredictor, RecognitionPredictor, and TableRecPredictor.
  • Output schemas return structured blocks (with html, label, polygon, bbox, reading_order, confidence); layout boxes include count (token budget estimate); table recognition returns full HTML tables (<table>...</table> with colspan / rowspan).
